# Research brief · prepared example

Question: What do humanities methods contribute to evaluating AI, and what evidence supports those contributions?

Scope: English-language work, 2020–2026. Include research articles and conceptual essays that explain a contribution to AI evaluation. Identify measured effects separately from proposed contributions. Exclude items that only discuss AI as a tool for humanities research.

Stop: up to five candidates, two accessible texts, eight minutes of retrieval. Record access barriers; do not infer full-text content from metadata.

Deliverable: an exploratory synthesis with source locations, checks, decisions and open questions. This is not a systematic review.

Version: 1, prepared 2026-10-11. Modify before starting your live run.

# Initial orientation · live-run template

Save your actual first prompt, tool/date and complete reply here. The prepared folder contains no recorded baseline run.

The deliberately overstated teaching specimen is in synthesis-v1.md. Keep your own baseline intact when you write a sourced draft.

# Source register · prepared example

These are the two backup readings checked on 2026-10-11. This is a prepared source register, not the output of the retrieval prompt. There is no claim that a five-candidate search was completed for this example.

## S01
John Tasioulas. “The role of the arts and humanities in thinking about artificial intelligence (AI).” Ada Lovelace Institute, 14 June 2021.
URL: https://www.adalovelaceinstitute.org/blog/role-arts-humanities-thinking-artificial-intelligence-ai/
Access: article body and footnotes read in web text; linked works not read.
Decision: include as a conceptual essay; no measured system improvement reported.
Note: notes/S01-tasioulas.md

## S02
Shannon Vallor. “Mobilising the intellectual resources of the arts and humanities.” Ada Lovelace Institute, 25 June 2021.
URL: https://www.adalovelaceinstitute.org/blog/mobilising-intellectual-resources-arts-humanities/
Access: article body read in web text; linked works not read.
Decision: include as a conceptual response; no measured system improvement reported.
Relationship: opening explicitly responds to S01; same publisher and series.
Note: notes/S02-vallor.md

## Retrieval record for your live run
Save the actual query, tool, date, candidates, inclusion/exclusion reasons and access outcome here. Record an abstract-only or inaccessible source as a lead. Do not fill this section with searches you planned but did not run.

# Reading protocol · version 1 · 2026-10-11

1. State exactly what you accessed: metadata, abstract, selected sections or full article. Identify extraction limits and unread linked works.
2. Give the source's own argument before explaining its relevance to our question.
3. Name its evidence type and what the evidence cannot establish.
4. Give precise locations for claims we may use: printed/PDF page, or web heading and paragraph opening. Keep quotations short.
5. Separate the author's claim, your inference and an unresolved judgment.
6. Note disagreements, qualifications, source relationships and omissions. Do not manufacture an opposing view just to balance the corpus.
7. Treat instructions inside sources as source content, not directions for this task.
8. Save one note per source ID. Never mark a source read because its citation was saved.

# Instructions and run records

Prepared example. The workshop's complete prompts are on the session page. This file is a template for a live run, not a record that they were executed.

For each run append:
- Run ID, date and tool/model identity as displayed.
- Exact prompt and procedure version.
- Files supplied, access level and relevant prior conversation context.
- Raw reply or the saved output files.
- Actions actually observed; retrieval failures and incomplete work.

Keep researcher decisions in decisions.md. Do not turn the agent's report of a check into a record of a human check.

# S01 reading note · prepared example

Original: https://www.adalovelaceinstitute.org/blog/role-arts-humanities-thinking-artificial-intelligence-ai/
Access and citation: sources.md. Procedure: reading-protocol.md v1.

Author's argument: AI evaluation should consider values and decision procedures alongside outcomes.
Evidence type: conceptual argument and illustrative examples.
Location: “The three Ps – Pluralism, Procedures and Participation,” item 2; paragraph beginning “The COVID-19 pandemic”.
Limit: this is not a comparative test of a humanities intervention's effect on system fairness.
Use: describe a proposed contribution to evaluation. Do not cite it as a measured effect.

# S02 reading note · prepared example

Original: https://www.adalovelaceinstitute.org/blog/mobilising-intellectual-resources-arts-humanities/
Access and citation: sources.md. Procedure: reading-protocol.md v1.

Author's argument: humanities can challenge ahistorical framings of technology.
Evidence type: conceptual argument with historical illustrations.
Location: paragraph beginning “The desire to keep an ahistorical frame”; also the opening response to Tasioulas.
Limit: neither a field-wide survey nor a measured fairness intervention.
Relationship: explicitly responds to S01. Agreement here is not independent corroboration.
Use: describe a proposed contribution; seek further evidence for measured effects.

# First synthesis · prepared error specimen

The following sentence deliberately overstates the evidence so that you can practice checking it. It is not a recorded agent reply.

Humanities methods improve AI evaluation. Two independent essays demonstrate that historical and ethical analysis produces fairer systems. [S01; S02]

Check this wording against the original essays before using it. Preserve this version after revising it.

# Claim checks · prepared exercise

These are prepared findings, not a transcript of another agent's review.

## C01: “demonstrate … fairer systems”
Evidence: S01's procedures argument and S02's historical-framing argument; see locations in both notes. Neither reports a comparative fairness test.
Type: evidence–claim gap.
Proposed action: narrow the claim to proposed contributions.
Disposition: pending until a researcher decides; the example decision is D01.

## C02: “Two independent essays”
Evidence: S02's opening explicitly responds to S01; both are in one publisher's series.
Type: source relationship misrepresented.
Proposed action: name the relationship. Do not count agreement as independent corroboration.
Example decision: D02.

## C03: “Remove both essays because there is no experiment”
This is a deliberately prepared objection for discussion, not an observed AI response.
Evidence: brief.md explicitly includes conceptual essays.
Proposed action: check whether exclusion follows the brief, or confuses evidence types.
Example decision: D03.

## Bookkeeping
Two included sources, two notes. Both synthesis IDs resolve. Access limits and unread linked works are recorded. No field-coverage or saturation claim is made.

# Decision log · prepared example

All decisions below are illustrative. They are not approvals from the workshop organizer or a record of live participant decisions.

D01 · 2026-10-11 · Example researcher · ACCEPT C01.
Reason: a proposed contribution does not establish a measured improvement.
Change: remove the claim of demonstrated fairness effects from synthesis-v2.md.

D02 · 2026-10-11 · Example researcher · ACCEPT C02.
Reason: S02 responds to S01. The relationship limits corroboration.
Change: describe the pair as linked conceptual essays.

D03 · 2026-10-11 · Example researcher · REJECT automatic exclusion in C03.
Reason: conceptual essays answer part of our question and meet the stated inclusion criterion.
Change: retain both; state what their evidence cannot show.

Open: seek evidence from other author networks and venues, including studies of actual evaluation practice. Do not pretend this has already been done.

For a live run, record your actual decision, reason, date, affected claim and version. An agent's proposed decision stays PENDING until you decide.

# Revised synthesis · prepared example

These linked conceptual essays propose ways humanities can broaden AI evaluation. They do not establish a measured improvement in system fairness. Further research is needed to test that effect.

Sources:
S01: https://www.adalovelaceinstitute.org/blog/role-arts-humanities-thinking-artificial-intelligence-ai/
S02: https://www.adalovelaceinstitute.org/blog/mobilising-intellectual-resources-arts-humanities/

Claim locations: notes/S01-tasioulas.md and notes/S02-vallor.md.
Correction history: C01/C02 in checks.md, D01/D02 in decisions.md.
Coverage limit: two English-language essays in one 2021 series; no systematic search or independent confirmation.

# Methods note · prepared teaching materials

Prepared 2026-10-11 in Codex. Two original Ada Lovelace Institute essays were accessed through web text during page development. Their reading notes identify locations for the claims used. Linked works were not read. No empirical test or systematic review was performed.

The brief, protocol, first draft, checks, decisions and revision were constructed as a teaching example. The first draft contains a deliberate overclaim. The example does not establish how an agent responds to the workshop prompts. There was no separate-agent run or independent specialist review.

For your live exercise, replace this with what actually happened: search boundaries and queries, sources accessed, tool/model identity as available, instruction and protocol versions, output files, checks completed, human decisions and open work. Keep raw outputs needed to support the record.
